translations.text: Then the great day of the mighty Lord will fall upon the earth-dwellers with terror, crashing in with force at midnight upon the bright creation, as a treacherous robber often does,
a thief who boldly goes about in darkness, in the black night, and suddenly seizes careless men bound in sleep, and brings evil on men who are unprepared.
So a great and mighty host, faithful to the Creator, will come up together on Mount Zion, bright and glad. Glory will be given to them!

Then from the four corners of the world, the farthest bounds of the earthly kingdom, angels shining all-bright will blow their trumpets together with a loud blare. The world will tremble, the ground beneath men.
Strong and clear, they will sound together toward the course of the stars. They will sing and make music from south and north, from east and west, over all creation.
They will wake from death the children of men, all mankind, to the appointed judgement, terrifyingly, out of the old earth; they will bid them stand up quickly from that fast sleep.
There one may hear a sorrowing people, sad at heart and harshly driven, anxiously lamenting the deeds of the living, terrified with fear.
That will be the greatest of signs ever shown to men, before or since, when the [?] host of angels and devils will be mingled together, the bright and the dark.
Both will come, the white and the black, as different homes have been made for them, for angels and for devils.

Then suddenly upon Mount Zion, from the south-east, a light like the sun's will come from the Creator, shining brighter than men can conceive in their minds, gleaming brightly, when the Son of God appears here through the vaults of the heavens.

The wondrous countenance of Christ will come, the beauty of the noble King, from the east out of the skies: sweet in spirit to his own people, bitter to the wicked, wondrously varied, different to the blessed and to the wretched.
To the good he will be gracious to look upon, beautiful, delightful to the holy company, fair in joy, friendly and loving,

lovely and gentle for the beloved to behold, that shining beauty, mild with good will, the coming of the Ruler, the mighty King, for those who before had pleased him well in mind, in words and in deeds.
To the evil he will be terrible and grim to behold, to sinful men, those who come there with their crimes, utterly condemned.
That may serve as a warning of punishment to anyone who has a wise mind, that he fears nothing at all who does not become frightened in spirit for terror before that countenance,

Then he will see the Lord of all creation coming in person to the assembly with many mighty wonders. On every side of him a troop of heavenly angels will move around him, a company of all-bright ones, hosts of holy ones in great throngs.
The deep creation will resound, and before the Lord the greatest of surging fires will sweep over the wide earth.
The hot flame will roar, the heavens will burst apart, firm and bright as they were; the stars will fall down.
Then the sun will be turned dark, changed to the colour of blood, the sun that shone brightly on the children of men over the former world;
The moon likewise, which before gave light to mankind by night, will fall down, and the stars likewise will be scattered from heaven, beaten by storms through the violent air.
The Almighty, Ruler of mighty kings, the glorious Prince, will come to the assembly with his band of angels. A triumphant company of his thanes will also be there.
Holy souls will travel with their Lord, when the Guardian of peoples himself comes to the nations of the earth with terrible punishment.

Throughout the wide earth the voice of the heavenly trumpet will be heard loudly, and on seven sides the winds will roar; they will blow, shattering, with the greatest of tumults; they will stir up and lay waste the world with storm, and fill the creatures of the earth with terror.
Then a hard crash will be heard, loud and immense, heavy and violent, the greatest of din, terrible to men.
There the accursed multitude of mankind will pass in crowds into the wide flame, where the deadly fire will find them alive, some up and some down, full of flame.
Then there is no doubt that Adam's race, full of cares, a sad people, will lament in grief, not over small things but over the greatest of mighty distresses,
when the dark surge of fire, the black flame, seizes all three together far and wide: the seas with their fish, the earth with her hills, and the bright heaven above with its stars.
The destroying flame will burn with force all three at once, grimly together. All the world will groan, afflicted, at that great hour.

So the greedy spirit will search through the depths. The ravaging flame will fell high buildings to the ground with the terror of fire. The far-spreading blaze [will sweep] the whole world, hot and fiercely greedy. Shattered city walls will fall in great numbers.
Mountains will melt, and high cliffs, which before had firmly shielded the land against the sea, against the floods, stiff and steadfast, foundations against the wave, against the winding water.
Then the death-flame will seize every creature, beasts and birds; the fire-black flame will travel across the earth, a raging warrior.
Where waters flowed before, the rushing floods, the sea-fish will then burn in a bath of fire. Cut off from the sea, every creature of the waves will die exhausted. The water will burn like wax.
There will be more wonders than anyone could conceive in mind, how the din and the storm and the violent air will shatter the broad creation.
Men will lament, weep, moaning with weary voices, abject, sad at heart, afflicted with sorrows.
The black flame will boil away sins in the doomed, and embers will swallow up ornaments of gold, all the ancient treasure of the kings of the land.
There will be clamour and care and the struggle of the living, grief and loud weeping at the heavenly destruction, the wretched suffering of men.
No one stained with wicked deeds can win peace from there or escape the burning anywhere on earth, but the fire will seize everything throughout the earth,
digging grimly and searching eagerly through the regions of the earth, inside and out, until the gleam of the fire has burned up with its surge all the stain of the world's defilement.
Then mighty God, King of the heavenly angels, will come to the famous mountain with the greatest power and majesty. He will shine holy and glorious above the hosts, God the Ruler,
and around him the noblest host, the holy troop, will shine brightly, the blessed company of angels. In their inmost thoughts they tremble, afraid, before the terror of the Father.
Therefore it is no wonder that the unclean race of worldly men, troubled with cares, should dread him harshly, when the holy race,
…white and bright as heaven, the host of high angels will be terrified with dread before that face; the bright creatures will wait, trembling, for the Lord's judgment.

The most terrible of days will come in the world, when the King of glory in his majesty will punish every nation. He will command those who have speech to rise from their graves in the earth, every single people, to come to the assembly, every one of mankind.

Then all the race of Adam will quickly take on flesh, and their rest in the earth, their time in that dwelling, will come to an end. Then each one must rise alive before the coming of Christ, take on limbs and body, and be young again.
Each will have on him everything, good or evil, that he loaded onto his soul on earth in days of old, over the course of the years. He will have both together, body and soul.
The appearance of each one's works, and the memory of their words, and the thoughts of the heart must come to light before the King of the heavens.
Then mankind will be increased and renewed by the Creator. A great host of people will rise to judgment, once the Author of life loosens the bond of death.
The sky will be set on fire, the stars of heaven will fall, greedy flames will spread far and wide, and spirits will pass to their eternal home. Men's deeds will be laid open across the world.
Men cannot conceal anything of their hoard, the thoughts of the heart, from the Ruler.
Their deeds will not be hidden. On that great day the Lord will know how each man earned eternal life before, and everything they did in the world, earlier or later, will be present there.
Nothing of men's thoughts will be concealed there. That great day will reveal all of it: the hoard locked in the breast, the thoughts of the heart.

Whoever means to bring a bright face to God must think beforehand of his soul's need, when the burning, hot and fiercely greedy, tests how well souls have been kept against sins before the victorious Judge.
when the voice of the trumpet and the bright sign, and the hot fire and the high host, and the majesty of angels and the affliction of terror, and the hard day and the high cross,
[?] raised upright as a sign of the kingdom; they summon before [it] the host of men, every soul of those who, later or earlier, received limbs in a body.

Then the greatest of hosts, eternal and young again, will go before the Ruler, present there both willingly and by necessity, each called by name. They will carry the hoard of their breasts, the treasures of their lives, before the Son of God.
The Father will consider how sound are the souls that his sons bring from the land in which they lived.

Then those who bring a bright face to the Creator will be confident. Their power and joy will be greatly blessed, a reward for their souls, a glorious reward for their works. It is well for those who, in that grim time, are able to please God.
There the sinful men themselves, sorrowful in mind, will see the greatest of sorrows.

It will be no grace to them that there before the nations the cross of our Lord stands present. It is the brightest of beacons, drenched in blood, the pure blood of the King of heaven, covered over with gore, and it shines brightly over the wide creation.
Shadows will be hidden where the bright tree shines upon the people.
Yet that will turn into harm and punishment for the nations, for those evildoers who gave God no thanks that he was hanged on the holy tree for the wicked deeds of mankind,
where on that day the Prince lovingly bought life for mankind with that price, his body, which did no stain of sinful crimes. With that he redeemed us.
For this he will sternly demand repayment for everything, when the red cross shines over all the sky in the place of the sun.

Upon it the fearful ones, ruined by their crimes, the black sinners, will gaze in sorrow; they will see, to their harm, what had come to them as their greatest good, if they had been willing to perceive it as good.
And they will also see, sad at heart, the old wounds and the open gashes on their Lord: how the hostile-minded drove nails through his white hands and his holy feet,
and likewise made blood flow from his side, where blood and water came out both together before the sight of their eyes, running before men, when he was on the cross.
Then they will be able to see all this for themselves, open and plain: that he suffered much for love of men, of sinners.
The children of men may clearly perceive how, false in their thoughts, they called him a liar, mocked him with insulting words, and also spat their spittle on his face.

They spoke scorn to him, and men eager for hell also struck his blessed face with their hands, with open palms and with fists too. Blind in their thoughts, foolish and deluded, they bent a hard crown of thorns around his head.

Then the mute creation saw it: the all-green earth and the heaven above fearfully felt the Lord's sufferings, and spoke with sorrow, though they were not living things, when their Creator suffered harm at sinful hands.
The sun was put out, darkened by affliction. Then the people in Jerusalem saw the finest of rich weavings, which the people had formerly been meant to look upon in the holy house, to its honour,

burst apart from the top down, so that it lay on the ground in two pieces. The veil of the temple, worked in wonderful colours to adorn the house, tore itself in two, as if the sharp edge of a knife had gone through it.
Walls and many stones across the land split cleanly apart, and the earth too, troubled by terror, trembled with a great din,
and the broad sea showed the might of its power, broke from its bonds and surged up furiously onto the earth's embrace; and the stars, shining in their places, gave up their lovely brightness.
At that same time heaven clearly recognized who had gloriously adorned it, made it bright with star-gems. That is why he sent his messenger when the shining king of creation was first born.
Lo, guilty men also truly saw, on the very day on which he suffered, a great wonder among the people: the earth gave up those who lay in it.
Those whom it had formerly held fast, buried dead, those who had kept the Lord's command in their hearts, rose up living again.
Hell too, the punisher of sins, perceived that the Creator had come, the ruling God, when it gave up that host, that band, from its hot breast.

Many people's minds were gladdened, and sorrow slipped away from their souls. Indeed, the sea also made known who had set it in its wide bed, the king mighty in glory: it made itself firm to walk on for him when God wished to go over its waves.

The ocean's stream did not dare to sink its Lord's feet in its flood; and the trees too, many and not few, made known who had shaped them with their blossoms, when mighty God climbed onto one of them, where he endured hardships for the need of the peoples of the earth, a hateful death as a help to humankind.
Then many a tree beneath its bark was drenched with bloody tears, red and thick; its sap turned to blood.
Dwellers on earth cannot tell, for all their wise understanding, how much those dead creatures, which cannot feel, perceived of the Lord's sufferings.
The noblest of earth's kinds of creatures, and heaven's lofty buildings too, all grew sad because of that one, seized with fear.
Though by their nature they had no understanding of mind, they were nevertheless wondrously changed when their Ruler departed from his body.
The people, men blind of mind and harder than flint, could not recognize the Lord, that the Lord, almighty God, had saved them from the torment of hell by his holy powers.

Yet from the very first, from the beginning of the world, far-seeing men, the Lord's prophets, holy and wise of mind, had told people this through their wise understanding, often and not just once, concerning that noble child:
that the precious stone, the Possessor of glory, the source of bliss, would become in the world a shelter and a comfort for all the human race, through the noble queen.

What can he hope for who will not thoughtfully remember the gentle teaching of the Lord, and all the hardships he endured for mankind because he wished that we might possess the homeland of glory in eternity?
So it will be grievous on that grim day of the great judgement for the one who, ruined by deadly sins, must look upon the Lord's wounds, his wounding and torment.

In weary mind they see the greatest of sorrows: how the king himself, with his own body and through his gentle heart, redeemed them from sins, so that they might live free of evil works and possess the eternal splendour of glory.

They did not know to give their ruler thanks for that homeland. So there, the unblessed ones, they see to their injury the signs plain upon God, when Christ sits on his royal throne, on the high seat, God of the heavenly hosts, the Father almighty.
The shining Creator, the Ruler of the heavens, will give judgement to every people according to their deeds, all according to what is right.
Then the pure peoples will be gathered on the right hand, chosen by Christ himself for their virtues, those who earlier, in the days of their life, eagerly and gladly carried out his word;
and there the wicked will be separated off before the Creator into the worse portion: the true King of victories will order the host of sinners to go away to the left hand.
There, convicted, they weep and tremble in fear before the Lord. They are an unclean people, as foul as goats, and they expect no mercy.

Then the judgement of souls will be decided before God for the generations of men, according to what they did before. There on the blessed three signs together will be plainly seen, because they kept their Lord's will well in word and deed.
The first is that it is plain to see there that they shine with light before the peoples, glorious and bright, over the dwellings of the cities.
Their former deeds shine on them, on each one of them, brighter than the sun.

The second, in addition, is likewise to be perceived: that they know the Ruler's gift is theirs in glory, and they look upon it, a joy to their eyes, knowing that in the kingdom of heaven they, blessed, may possess pure joys with the angels.

Then the third is how that blessed host sees the condemned in the evil of darkness suffer pain as punishment for their sins: the surging flame, and the tearing of serpents with bitter jaws, a crowd of the burning.
From this a delightful joy grows in them, when they see others endure the evil that they themselves escaped through the Lord's mercy.

Then they thank God all the more eagerly for the glory and the bliss, both of which they see: that he saved them from deadly torment and also granted them eternal joys. Hell is shut to them, the kingdom of heaven given.
So shall it be repaid to those who before kept the Lord's will well through love of heart.
Then for the others it will turn out unlike their wish. They may see far too many woes upon themselves, sin enough, terrible wicked deeds committed before.
There pain clings to them in their sorrow, misery, great calamity, on three sides.
The first of these is that they see far too many miseries present before them, the grim fire of hell ready for their punishment, in which they must forever, struggling in torment, endure damnation.
Then the second hardship is likewise a disgrace to them, the guilty: that there, condemned, they endure the greatest shame.
On them the Lord sees not just a few loathsome crimes, and the all-bright army of heaven's angels also looks on that, and the children of men,
all earth-dwellers, and the terrible devil, the dark power: through the bodies they can see on the souls every stain of wickedness, the crimes of their vices.
The sinful flesh will be shot through with shames like clear glass, so that one can very easily see through it all.
Then the third sorrow for the wretched ones will be a lamenting grief, that they see the pure ones and how they joyfully rejoice for their good deeds,
Those things they, unhappy, scorned to do before, while their days lasted; and [they suffer] weeping pain for their deeds, because they freely did wrong before.

They see the better ones shine in glory. Their own misery alone is not their punishment; the happiness of the others is also a sorrow to them, because in former days they abandoned such fair and such peerless joys for the false pleasure of the body, the idle lust of the wretched flesh.
There, ashamed and overwhelmed by disgraces, they stagger in confusion; they bear the burden of sin, their wicked deeds, on which the peoples look.

It would then be better for them if they had earlier been ashamed of their evil deeds, of every wrong and of their base works, before one man, and had told God's messenger that they knew to their sorrow of the sinful deeds in themselves.
The confessor cannot see through the flesh into the soul, whether a man tells him truth or lies about himself when he confesses his sin.
Yet a person can heal every sin, every unclean evil, if he confesses it to one man. On that hard day no one can hide an unatoned stain, where the hosts will see it.
Alas, if only we could now see the evil crimes in our souls, the wounds of sins, with the eyes of the body: the thoughts of vice, the unclean inner thoughts!
No one can tell another with how much zeal each person would strive by every skill to gain life, fearfully for his life, to endure from then on, to wash away the rust of sin and to chastise himself,

and to heal the stain of former wounds in the short time of life there is here, so that before the eyes of earth-dwellers he might, unashamed, enjoy his homeland among men without disgrace, while body and soul may live together.

Now we must eagerly and wisely look through the chambers of our breast with the eyes of the heart, at the vices within. With those other eyes, the jewels of the head, we cannot in any way see through to the spirit of the mind's thought,
whether evil or good dwells beneath it, so that one may please God in that grim time when he shines in glory from his high throne with bright flame over every host.
There the high king of the heavens will first speak, before the angels and before the nations, to the blessed ones, and graciously promise them peace:
With holy voice he comforts them kindly and offers them peace. He bids them go safe and blessed to the homeland of the angels' joy, and enjoy it as they wish forever:

"Receive now, with friends, my Father's kingdom, which was joyfully prepared for you before the ages: glory with bliss, the bright beauty of the homeland, where you may see the riches of life with those most dear, the sweet joys of heaven.
You earned this when you willingly received poor men, needy in the world, with a gentle heart.
When they humbly asked you for kindness in my name, then you helped them and gave them shelter, bread to the hungry and clothing to the naked;
and to those who lay sick in pain, faring hard, bound by disease, you faithfully turned your thought with the love of your heart."
You did all that to me when you visited them in kindness and strengthened their minds with comfort. For that you shall long enjoy a fair reward among those dear to you."
Then God, the ruler of all, will begin to speak in different words, with the terror of punishment, to the evil ones who are on his left hand.

They need not then hope for mercy from the Creator, nor for life nor favours; but there rewards will come to men, to those who have speech, according to the deserts of their words and deeds. They must undergo that just judgement alone, full of terror.

There the great mercy of the Almighty will be taken away from the peoples on that day, when he angrily charges that perverse people with their sins in hateful words, and commands them to show forth now the account of the life that he had once given them, sinful as they were, for their good.
The Lord almighty himself begins to speak as though he were speaking to one person, and yet he means them all, the sin-guilty people:
"Listen, O man: I first made you with my own hands and gave you understanding.
I formed your limbs from clay. I gave you a living spirit and honoured you above all creation. I made you have a face and a form like mine.
I also gave you abundance of powers and wealth over every wide land; you knew no share of woe, of darkness, that you would have to suffer. You showed no thanks for this.
When I had shaped you so beautiful, made you delightful, and given you wealth so that you might rule over the creatures of the world,
when I set you in that fair land to enjoy the bright abundance of paradise, shining with colours, then you would not keep the word of life, but broke my command at the word of your slayer.
You obeyed the treacherous fiend, the harmful ravager, more than your Creator.
Now I pass over the old story of how you first set your mind on evil, and by sinful works lost what I had given you for your benefit.

When I had given you so many good things, and in your mind there seemed too little happiness in all of them if you could not possess power equal to God's, then you became estranged from that joy, cast far away, to the delight of fiends.
You were forced to give up, sad at heart, the beauty of paradise, the homeland of spirits, wretched and dejected, deprived of all good things and joys, and then you were driven into this dark world.
There you afterwards suffered great hardships for a long time: pain, grievous struggle and dark death. After your passing you had to fall, abject and without any helper, into hell.
Then I began to grieve that my handiwork should pass into the power of fiends, that the offspring of mankind should see death and have to explore an unknown land, painful journeys.
Then I myself descended, a child into a mother, though her virginity remained wholly intact. I alone was born as a comfort to the peoples.
Hands wrapped me and covered me with the garments of the poor, and then laid me in darkness, wound in dark cloths. Lo, I endured that for the world's sake!
I seemed of little worth to the children of men; I lay on hard stone, a young child in a crib.
Because I wished to take death away from you, and the hot torment of hell, so that you might shine holy and blessed in the eternal life, I endured that hardship.
It was not for my own pleasure, but in my youth I endured misery and cruel bodily pain, so that through it I might be like you, and you might become like my own beauty, free from sin.
And for love of mankind my head suffered harmful blows. My cheek endured them, and my face often received the spittle from the mouths of impious men and evildoers.
Likewise they bitterly mixed together for me an unsweet drink of vinegar and gall.
When I suffered the hostility of enemies before the people, they persecuted me wickedly, cared nothing for the guilt of their enmity, and struck me with whips.
I endured all that pain for you in humility, the scorn and the harsh words. Then they bent a sharp, hard crown around my head and pressed it down with violence. It was made of thorns.

When I was hung on the high tree, fastened to the cross, when they quickly poured the blood out of my side with a spear, gore onto the ground, it was so that through that you might be saved from the devil's tyranny.
Then I, without stain, suffered torment and evil hardships, until I alone sent forth the living spirit from my body.
See now the mortal wounds that you dealt before on my hands and on my feet as well, by which I hung, cruelly fastened. Here you can also see, still plain now, the bloody wound in my side.
How unequal was the reckoning between us two!

I took on your pain so that you, blessed and happy, might enjoy my native kingdom. With my death I bought for you, at great cost, that long life, so that afterwards you might dwell in light, beautiful and without stain.
My body, which had harmed no one, lay buried in the earth, hidden below in the tomb, so that you might be bright up in the heavens, powerful among the angels.
Why did you forsake that bright life which I, out of love, faithfully revealed to you with my body as a help to the wretched?
Have you become so senseless that you did not know to thank the Ruler for your redemption?
I do not ask anything now about my bitter death, which I endured for you. But repay me your life, for which I once gave my own as its price through worldly torment.
I claim that life which you have sinfully slain with your vices, to your own shame.
Why have you, of your own will, foully defiled through wicked lusts and filthy sin that dwelling which I hallowed in you as dear to me, a house for joy?
And you, working sin, defiled with shameful deeds the body that I had redeemed for myself from the grasp of fiends, and then forbade it to sin.
Why have you hung me more heavily on the cross of your hands than I hung before? Truly, this one seems harder to me!
Now the cross of your sins, on which I am fastened against my will, is heavier upon me than the other was, which I mounted before of my own will,
when your misery grieved me most deeply at heart, when I drew you out of hell, if only you had been willing to keep it afterwards yourself.
I was a beggar in the world so that you might become rich in heaven; I was poor in your homeland so that you might become blessed in mine.
Yet in your mind you gave no thanks at all to your Saviour for all of this.
I commanded you to treat my brothers well in the earthly kingdom, out of the possessions I gave you on earth, and to help the poor.
You carried that out wretchedly. You refused the needy any chance to come in under your roof, and with hard hearts you denied them everything: clothing to the naked, food to the hungry.
Though they, weary and sick, asked you in my name for water, tormented for want of drink, without means, overcome by thirst, you boldly refused them.
You did not seek out the sorrowful, nor speak a kind word of comfort to them, so that they might take heart with a gladder mind.
All that you did to me, to the humiliation of the King of heaven. For this you must harshly endure torment for ever and ever, and suffer exile among devils."
Then the Guardian of victories himself will send forth over them all a terrible sentence, full of pain, upon the doomed people. He will say to the company of the sinful souls:

"Go now, accursed ones, cut off by your own will from the joy of the angels, into the eternal fire that was prepared for Satan and his companions with him, for the devil and the dark band, hot and fiercely grim. Into that you must fall!"
Then, robbed of all counsel, they cannot disobey the command of the King of heaven. Those who strove against God before must quickly fall into the grim abyss.
Then the Guardian of the kingdom will be stern and mighty, angry and terrible. No enemy on this earthly path can stand before him and endure him.

With his right hand he will sweep with the sword of victory, so that the devils fall into the deep pit, into the black flame: the host of the sinful under the surface of the earth, the doomed spirits into the dwelling of the hostile ones, the accursed troop of the wicked, to destruction in the house of torment, the devil's hall of death.

Never afterwards will they seek remembrance of the Lord, nor will they escape from their sin, where, stained with crimes and bound in flame, they suffer death. The punishment for their sin will be present to them and unconcealed; that is eternal death.

That hot portion of the race of hell, in perpetual night, cannot burn away sin, the stain from the soul, forever; but there the deep pit feeds the wretched ones, the bottomless one holds the spirits in darkness,
It will burn them with the ancient fire and with the terrible frost, and torment the peoples with fierce serpents and many punishments, with deadly jaws.

so that we may consider and say with one voice, and speak the truth: that a man has lost the guardian of the soul, the wisdom of life, if he does not care now whether his spirit will be wretched or blessed in the place where, after his departure, he must dwell forever.
The heedless man does not fear to commit sin, and he feels no remorse at all in his mind that the Holy Spirit is leaving him because of his sins in this passing time.
when the wicked criminal, afraid before the Creator, stands dark at the judgment, stained with death, cursed with his sins; the traitor will be filled with fire.

Unworthy of life, oppressed by terror, standing before God, he bears, dark and without beauty, the colour of the accursed, the mark of deceit on his life. Then the children of sin will pour out tears, when it is not the time for it, and lament their sins;
but they do it too late to help their souls, when the Ruler of hosts will not heed how the wicked bitterly lament their old treasures at that time when all is revealed.
In that time of sorrows it will not be granted to people that anyone may find a remedy there, if he now will not gain salvation for his life while he lives here.
There no grief will be shown to any of the good, nor any good to any of the evil, but there each will carry before him his own deserts, plainly in view.
Therefore whoever wishes to have life with the Creator must hurry, while light and spirit are still bound together in him.

Let him care eagerly for the beauty of his soul according to God's will, and let him be careful in his words and deeds, his habits and thoughts, while this world, moving with its shadows, may still shine on him,

so that in this passing time he does not lose the glory of his joy and the count of his days, the beauty of his work and the reward of glory, which the faithful King of heaven gives at the holy time as rewards of victory to those who eagerly obey him in their spirits.
Then heaven and hell will be filled with the children of men, the souls of human beings.

The depths will swallow God's adversaries, the leaping flame the hateful men; it will torment the criminals and never let them go from there into joy, to the salvation of life, but the burning will bind the host fast in waiting, and will hate the children of sin.
It seems terrible to me that these spirit-bearers, men, will not think in their minds, when they do evil, about the punishment the Ruler has set for them, for the hateful people.
Then life and death will swallow up souls. The house of torments will stand open and be revealed to the oath-breakers, and wicked men will fill it with their dark souls.
Then, as punishment for their sins, the crowd of the guilty will be cut off in disgrace from the holy ones and sent to painful death.
There thieves and criminals, liars and adulterers, must not hope for life, and perjurers will see the reward of their murderous deeds, hard and fiercely grim.
Then hell will take the host of the faithless, and the Ruler will give them to the fiends for destruction; the guilty will suffer terrible, deadly torment.
Wretched is the man who wants to commit crimes, so that, guilty, he must be cut off from his Creator on Judgment Day and sent down to death,
down among hell's [?], into the hot fire, under the lock of flame, where they stretch out their limbs to be bound and burned and scourged as punishment for their sins.
Then, by the power of God and at the King's word, the Holy Spirit will lock up hell, the greatest of houses of murder, full of fire, together with the army of devils.
That will be the greatest of torments for devils and men! That is a joyless house, where no one can ever escape from the cold fetters.

They broke the King's word, the bright command of the books. Therefore those who here scorned the majesty of the kingdom of heaven must remain in endless night, stained by their wicked deeds, and suffer endless pain forever.

Then the chosen will bear bright adornments before Christ. Their glory will live on at Doomsday; they will possess with God the joy of a gentle life, which is granted to each of the holy in the kingdom of heaven.

That is the homeland that will never come to an end. There, free from sin, they will dwell in joy forever and praise the Lord, the beloved guardian of life. They will be wrapped in light, clothed in peace, protected from sorrows, honored with joys, and faithful to the Lord.
For ever and ever they will joyfully enjoy the company of angels, shining with grace, and they will love the guardian of the people. The Father of all has power and rules over the host of the holy.
There is the song of angels, the bliss of the blessed; there is the precious face of the Lord, brighter than the sun to all the blessed.

There is the love of dear ones, life without the death that ends it, a glad host of people, youth without age, the glory of the heavenly hosts, health without pain, rest without strife for those who do right,

There the blessed will have day without darkness, bright and full of glory, joy without sorrow, peace among friends forever without envy for the blessed in heaven, and harmony without hostility in the company of the saints.

There is no hunger or thirst there, no sleep or serious sickness, no burning of the sun, no cold and no care. Instead, the company of the blessed, the most beautiful of hosts, will enjoy the King's gifts forever, in glory with the Lord.
